title: JFK
events_chronological: Newsreel footage lays out the Kennedy presidency, the Bay of Pigs and the Cuban missile crisis.
On 22 November 1963 President Kennedy is shot in Dealey Plaza in Dallas.
Officer J.D. Tippit is shot dead nearby, and Lee Harvey Oswald is arrested in a cinema and charged with both killings.
Oswald denies everything, calls himself a patsy, and is shot by Jack Ruby in the basement of police headquarters.
New Orleans district attorney Jim Garrison notices Oswald's local connections and interviews the pilot David Ferrie.
The FBI takes the case away from Garrison, and he lets it go for three years.
The Warren Commission publishes its single-bullet conclusion and twenty-six volumes of supporting evidence.
In 1966 Garrison reads the Warren Report, finds it unbelievable, and reopens the investigation with his own staff.
Garrison's team retrace Oswald's summer in New Orleans, his Fair Play for Cuba leafleting and his links to Guy Banister's office at 544 Camp Street.
Witnesses describe shots from the grassy knoll, men flashing badges behind the fence, and a rifle in a window.
Ferrie, terrified and drinking, tells Garrison he is a dead man, and is found dead a few days later.
Willie O'Keefe, in prison, describes a party at which Clay Bertrand, Ferrie and Oswald discussed killing Kennedy.
Garrison meets a man called X in Washington, who describes how the President's security was stripped, who stood to gain, and how such an operation would be run.
Garrison charges the businessman Clay Shaw with conspiracy, identifying him as Clay Bertrand.
The press turns on Garrison, his staff resign, his marriage nearly collapses, and his witnesses die or recant.
At trial Garrison runs the Zapruder film over and over and argues the physical impossibility of the single-bullet theory.
Garrison delivers a closing address to the jury about a coup d'etat and about telling the truth.
The jury acquits Clay Shaw in under an hour while accepting that there was a conspiracy.
Closing captions record that Shaw's CIA connection emerged later, and that files remain sealed until 2029.
syuzhet_notes: The film's present is Garrison's investigation and trial, and nearly everything else arrives as reconstruction: told-order bullets 1-4 are newsreel and staged history, and bullets 9-12 are witness accounts staged as flashback, often in several mutually incompatible versions of the same afternoon. Told-order bullet 14, the meeting with X, is a long flashback inside a flashback, and the film cuts speculative footage into documentary material throughout without marking where one ends and the other begins.
fabula_notes: Much of what is dramatised is conjecture presented as reconstruction - the film stages several versions of the shooting, only one of which can be true - so this chronology follows the account Garrison assembles rather than an established record. The meeting with X and several of the witness scenes are composites invented for the film.
